segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So we've seen how with orders we want to use this mood tense with the exception of positive orders which are informal. There we have a shortcut: we can just cut off the 's' of the informal form. For example, what is to wait?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Esperar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And what is you wait, informally?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Esperas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esperas. And wait, the order?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Espera.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Espera. That's our shortcut. How would you say let's wait?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Esperemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Esperemos, good. And you can also say esperamos; it just sounds less like an order, it would sound more like shall we wait? ¿Esperamos? Shall we wait? But then the order: esperemos. Let's not wait.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No esperemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No esperemos, good. So the orders we are using with you—the different versions of you—and with we. But maybe I want to say what I want him to do or what I want her to do or what I want them to do. Other than the structures that we learned already—quiero que, prefiero que, etcetera—we can just say que and follow it with the subjunctive. So, for example, maybe you tell me David is waiting for you, and I say ¡que espere! ¡Que espere!

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: That he waits. But I'm using this mood tense, so I'm saying let him wait. Let him wait. ¡Que espere!

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Maybe I really want the show to finish. I want the show to hurry up and finish. I can say que it finishes in the mood tense, and then I get that meaning of let it finish, hurry up and finish. So how would I say that: let it finish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Que termine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Que termine, good. Que termine. We said that the word for already was ya, and we can use that here. So, let it finish already.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Que termine ya.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Que termine ya. Enough already. We said that callarse was to quiet oneself or to shut up. So maybe you want somebody to shut up, you're not angry enough to tell them directly, maybe you will just say, "Oh, let them... let him shut up. Let him quiet himself." How would that be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Que se calle.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. ¡Que se calle! Another situation that we use the mood tense in is when after the word cuando we refer to the future. For example, if I say when we speak, and I mean generally, how will it sound?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando hablamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cuando hablamos. So this is generally, when we speak generally, and you could continue, no? But if you mean in a future event, when we speak later on, then you will use this mood tense. Now this is very interesting use of the mood tense because it highlights some kind of superstition maybe, that the language is uncomfortable with referring to something in the future that didn't happen yet as a fact. So you're putting this mood tense there to kind of highlight that subjectivity.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Give me when we speak then, when we speak, and we mean the future: when we speak.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando hablemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cuando hablemos. We are using this mood tense because we are referring to something that's going to happen in the future that we give it as a fact, and it's like who are we as mere mortals to do such a thing, to refer to this event or to this fact that will be? So, for example, you could say when we eat together, we speak. And you mean generally, no? When we eat together, we speak. What was together? Related to junction, related to joint, related to what in English they say military junta?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Junta.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say when we eat together, we speak, when we eat together, we speak?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando comemos junta...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Junta is the version you found through military junta, but you're not just going to take it, you're going to have to process it as well. When we eat together...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Juntas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you're two females, that's fine. So, cuando comemos juntas, we speak.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. All together: when we eat together, we speak.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando comemos juntas, hablamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cuando comemos juntas, hablamos. So here you're speaking generally, generalmente, generally, when we eat together we speak. But if you want to say when we eat together and you're referring to the future, a fact that you're naming that hasn't happened yet, there you want to use your mood tense. So let's work our way through it: when we eat together, and we're referring to the future...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando comamos juntas...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: We will speak. And we don't need 'will' with we will speak because the when we eat together is a future context; we can just go back to normal everyday present again.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Hablamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cuando comamos juntas—two females—when we eat together, hablamos, we will speak. Now hablamos is just normal present because it's not directly connected to cuando and we have future context already, so we can just use hablamos. So if we compare these two sentences, the only difference is in that mood tense: cuando comemos juntos hablamos—this means generally, I went back to male or mixed group—cuando comemos juntos hablamos (generally), cuando comamos juntos hablamos (when we eat together, we will speak).

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What is I go or I'm going?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Voy.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Voy. Now you could probably guess that the mood tense of voy and va and vamos is irregular. So the root is vaya, v-a-y-a, vaya, and then we add on our consonants if we need them. So, for example, the they form or the you plural form would be...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vayan.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vayan. We form?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vayamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Vayamos, good. So how would you say we see her when we go, and you're speaking generally: we see her...

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La vemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La vemos, when we go, generally speaking.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando vamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. La vemos cuando vamos. But if we want to say we will see her when we go, and we're referring to the future, not generally, we'll see her when we go, how would that be? So we will see her, we can just use the present because when we go is the future context. So again, how is we will see her?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La vemos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. When we go, and we refer now to the future with when we go?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando vayamos.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. La vemos cuando vayamos. So we have: la vemos cuando vamos (generally), la vemos cuando vayamos (in the future).
